reproach

rih-PROHCH -- from Old French reprochier, ultimately from Latin prope, 'near': a reproach brings blame close, almost thrown in someone's face. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Reproach is an expression of disapproval or disappointment, aimed at the person who caused it.

There was more reproach than anger in the librarian's sigh when she found the torn library book returned a year late.

Example

Rather than shouting, the veteran teacher simply looked at the empty seat where the missing homework should have been, and that single glance of quiet reproach felt worse than any lecture.

Reproach is often quiet rather than loud -- a disappointed look can express exactly the same disapproval as a shouted scolding, sometimes more effectively.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

criticism: Criticism points out what is wrong with something and can be completely impersonal -- a movie review is criticism. Reproach is personal and moral: it tells a particular person they have disappointed you. An editor criticizes a draft without ever knowing its author; a reproach needs a person on both ends.

disappointment: Disappointment is the feeling itself -- the sinking sense that someone let you down. Reproach is that feeling made visible and aimed at the person: a sigh, a quiet word, a pointed silence that says you should have done better. You can hide disappointment; a reproach is always delivered.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

approval: a feeling that something is good or acceptable

praise: an expression of admiration or approval

Where it sits · how personal and loud the displeasure gets

disapproval → reproach → scolding

disapproval vs. reproach: Disapproval is a broad, calm word for simply not liking something, while reproach adds a more personal note of disappointment aimed directly at someone.

scolding vs. reproach: Scolding is sharper and louder than reproach, which can be entirely silent -- a single disappointed look, not a single word said aloud.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: back, again, intensifier (Old French)

Root — proach: near (from Latin prope, 'near' -- the same piece you see in approach)

Put it together: Reproach comes from Old French reprochier: re- ('back, again') + proach ('near,' from Latin prope). To reproach someone is, at its root, to bring blame close to them -- the same root behind the word approach.

Use the root in a new word: approach: The pilot began her final approach to the runway as the storm clouds rolled in behind her.

Word Building

Word Choice

Reproach is a noun describing a milder, more personal expression of disappointment than an official "reprimand," and it lacks the formal, public weight of a "censure" -- all three appear in this unit.
